requirement.title: Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly
requirement.body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Given the following project structure:

 - Project A
    - `ProjectA.MyType`

 - Project B
    - References
        - Project A
    - Package References
        - MessagePack
    
I need to have a source-generated `IMessagePackFormatter` for type `ProjectA.MyType` generated **inside Project B** instead of Project A, because the latter has no (and cannot have) reference to MessagePack nuget package.

## Describe the solution you'd like

Add a `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute that will work for partial classes implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`.

For example:

```csharp
[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]
partial class MyObjectFormatter: IMessagePackFormatter<MyObject>;
```

That's it. The class does not even need to declare a body (no `{` and `}`), because the actual implementation is source-generated by `MessagePack.SourceGenerator.MessagePackGenerator` as usual.

As for the attribute-based property keys and other settings (such as Union), I can think of 3 alternatives:

1 - Use `System.Runtime.Serialization.DataMember` and related attributes. This is too limited IMO, as it cannot have `Union` and other features.

2 - Allow the generator and analyzers to work with user-defined versions of the MessagePack attributes. This would be similar to how you can declare dummy versions of BCL attributes that the C# compiler expects, such as [`[IsExternalInit]`](https://stackoverflow.com/a/67687186/643085) or `[ModuleInitializer]`. With this, I could simply copy and paste the attribute definitions for MessagePack attributes such as `[Key]` into my Project A, and have the source-generated formatter (as described above) pick them.

3 - Source-generate the attributes themselves using [`IncrementalGeneratorInitializationContext.RegisterPostInitializationOutput`](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/main/docs/features/incremental-generators.md#outputting-values) instead of them existing in the `MessagePack.Annotations` assembly. This would allow using the attributes without adding an additional runtime dependency. Only compile-time reference to the analyzer Nuget would be required.

## Motivation

Project A is really a library (Nuget package), and I really want to keep it minimal. It currently has zero dependencies and I would really like to keep it that way.

story.headline: A project that references MessagePack can now declare `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class XFormatter : IMessagePackFormatter<T>` for a type T from another assembly, and the source generator writes the formatter body and registers it in the generated resolver.
story.before: The source generator only wrote formatters for types in the current compilation that carried [MessagePackObject]. A type from a dependency-free library (Project A) could not get a generated formatter in Project B. The only options were a hand-written formatter or adding MessagePack to Project A.
story.after: Project B declares a partial formatter class with the new attribute. The generator fills in Serialize/Deserialize for T and adds the formatter to the generated resolver. If SurrogateType is not set, it uses all public read-write members of T with string keys. If SurrogateType is set, it takes [Key]/[IgnoreMember] from a surrogate type that Project B declares. Invalid declarations get errors MsgPack019–022 and produce no output.

steps.text: Add the public GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute (with an optional SurrogateType) to MessagePack.Annotations, plus generator constants for its name.
Define four new error diagnostics: formatter not partial (MsgPack019), not exactly one IMessagePackFormatter<T> (020), unsupported data type (021), surrogate member mismatch (022).

GeneratedFormatterCollector validates the formatter declaration and T. It then builds an ObjectSerializationInfo, either contractless (string keys over public read-write members) or from the surrogate's Key attributes, with members matched by name and type.

A new ForAttributeWithMetadataName pipeline feeds these requests into the model collection, so the resolver registers them. A second pipeline runs the collector again to report diagnostics. The existing hand-written formatter scan now skips attributed classes, so they are not registered twice.
ObjectSerializationInfo gets an IsUserDeclaredFormatter flag. When it is set, the int-key and string-key templates emit `partial class` so the output merges with the user's declaration.

A new ExternalTypes test assembly with no MessagePack reference backs the round-trip, wire-shape and resolver-registration tests, and generator tests cover the new diagnostics. The README and the analyzer docs describe the feature.

alsoTouches: ObjectSerializationInfo.Equals now compares IsUserDeclaredFormatter, so models that differ only in that flag are no longer equal for incremental caching.
Any class carrying [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] is dropped from the existing custom-formatter discovery, even if it has a hand-written body.
The generator runs GeneratedFormatterCollector twice per attributed class: once to build models and once to report diagnostics.
MapModeExecutionTests now excludes the new external-type test files from its compile set.

lines.s: Learn more about using a mix of your own custom formatters and automatically generated ones in [the Analyzer section](#analyzer).
### Formatters for types from other assemblies
A type that comes from an assembly you cannot change, such as a dependency-free library, may have no MessagePack attributes at all.
You can still get a source-generated formatter for it by declaring a `partial` formatter class in your own project and marking it with `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]`:
// ProjectA.MyObject lives in a library that does not reference MessagePack.
The source generator writes the body of `MyObjectFormatter`, and the generated `GeneratedMessagePackResolver` registers it automatically.
Nothing needs to be added to `ProjectA`.
By default the formatter serializes the type in *contractless* mode: every public, read-write instance property and field is serialized under its name as a string key.
Read-only members are skipped because they cannot be deserialized.
To control keys and membership without touching the type, name a *surrogate* type in the attribute.
The surrogate's `[Key]` and `[IgnoreMember]` attributes describe the wire contract, and its members are matched to members of the formatted type by name and type.
The surrogate is only read at compile time and is never instantiated.
When a surrogate is used, only the members it lists are serialized.
All of its keys must be integers or all must be strings.
- Only classes and structs are supported. Generic types, abstract types, and unions from other assemblies are not.

- Deserialization uses an accessible parameterless constructor (any struct can be created without one). Constructor parameters are not matched, so types that only have a parameterized constructor are not supported yet.
- Nested member types are not generated from the formatter. They are resolved through the other resolvers in your composite resolver, as usual.
- Formatter diagnostics are reported as `MsgPack019` through `MsgPack022`, listed in the [analyzers](doc/analyzers/index.md).

[MagicOnion](https://github.com/Cysharp/MagicOnion) is a code-first gRPC framework based on grpc-dotnet and MessagePack. gRPC usually communicates with Protocol Buffers using IDL. But MagicOnion uses MessagePack for C# and does not need IDL. When communicating C# to C#, schemaless (or rather C# classes as schema) is better than using IDL.
# MsgPack019 Generated formatter must be partial
A class marked with `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` is the target of source generation. The generator writes the body of the formatter into the class, so the class must be declared `partial`.
## Examples of patterns that are flagged by this analyzer
public class MyObjectFormatter : IMessagePackFormatter<ProjectA.MyObject> // Diagnostic reported here: not partial
Declare the class `partial` and leave its body empty:
Any nesting types that contain the formatter must also be declared `partial`.
# MsgPack020 Generated formatter must implement IMessagePackFormatter<T>
A class marked with `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` identifies the data type to serialize by its `IMessagePackFormatter<T>` interface. The class must implement exactly one such interface.
## Examples of patterns that are flagged by this analyzer
public partial class MyObjectFormatter // Diagnostic reported here: no IMessagePackFormatter<T>
Implement `IMessagePackFormatter<T>` for the type to be serialized:
# MsgPack021 Generated formatter data type not supported

The source generator writes formatters for non-generic, non-abstract classes and structs that the formatter can access. The data type named by the formatter's `IMessagePackFormatter<T>` interface must meet these requirements.
## Examples of patterns that are flagged by this analyzer
public partial class MyBaseFormatter : IMessagePackFormatter<MyBase> // Diagnostic reported here: abstract
public partial class ListFormatter : IMessagePackFormatter<List<int>> // Diagnostic reported here: generic
Use a concrete, non-generic class or struct as the data type. For an abstract base type, use [`[Union]`](../../README.md#union) with the derived types instead.
# MsgPack022 Surrogate member does not match the formatted type

When `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter(SurrogateType = typeof(...))]` is used, each keyed member of the surrogate must match a public, read-write instance member of the formatted type, with the same name and type.
## Examples of patterns that are flagged by this analyzer
// ProjectA.MyObject has `public int Id { get; set; }` and no `Missing` member.
public int Missing { get; set; } // Diagnostic reported here
Rename the surrogate member to match a public, read-write member of the formatted type, and make sure the types are identical:

findings.title: Key and ignore attributes on the formatted type are never read (AC4)
findings.body: The collector builds the member list for the formatted type from member names and accessibility only. It never reads attributes on that type: not [Key], not [IgnoreMember], not [DataMember]/[IgnoreDataMember], and not user-declared copies matched by name. AC4 asks the formatter to follow key settings declared on the type; here the only way to express keys is a parallel surrogate class in the consuming project. A member the type's author marked as ignored is serialized by default.
findings.scenario: Project A declares `class MyType { [DataMember(Name="id")] public int Id {get;set;} [IgnoreDataMember] public string Secret {get;set;} }`. Project B declares `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class F : IMessagePackFormatter<MyType> {}`. Output is a map with keys "Id" and "Secret": the declared name is ignored and the ignored member is written to the wire.
findings.suggestion: Either honour ignore/key attributes found on the formatted type (at minimum IgnoreMember, IgnoreDataMember, NonSerialized, and DataMember or name-matched Key), or get explicit sign-off that surrogate-only satisfies AC4 and document that attributes on the type are ignored.

findings.title: UseMapMode is ignored for surrogate int-keyed generated formatters
findings.body: For [MessagePackObject] types, TypeCollector forces string-key (map) output when the resolver has UseMapMode = true (TypeCollector.cs line 773). The new GeneratedFormatterCollector never reads options.Generator.Formatters.UsesMapMode: isIntKey comes only from the surrogate's key kind. In a map-mode project, a surrogate with integer keys therefore still emits an array, unlike the same type declared in-project (AC4). The MapMode execution test project explicitly excludes the new test files, so nothing exercises this combination.
findings.scenario: Project has `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver(UseMapMode = true)]` and `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter(SurrogateType = typeof(S))]` where S uses `[Key(0)]`/`[Key(1)]`. The generated formatter writes `WriteArrayHeader(2)`, while every [MessagePackObject] type in the same project writes maps.

refs.quote: <!-- GeneratedFormatterForExternalTypes*.cs need the ExternalTypes assembly, which this project does not reference. -->

findings.suggestion: Force isIntKey to false in Collect when options.Generator.Formatters.UsesMapMode is set, mirroring TypeCollector. Add the ExternalTypes reference to the MapMode test project instead of excluding the files, or add a generator test with UseMapMode = true.

findings.title: Formatter class shape is not validated; generic, abstract or badly nested formatters emit broken code
findings.body: Validation of the formatter class only checks that the class itself is partial and implements one IMessagePackFormatter<T>. A generic formatter class, an abstract one, a private nested one, or one nested in a non-partial outer type all pass. The resolver then emits `new <Formatter>()` and the template re-declares the outer types as `partial`, so the user gets raw compiler errors in generated code instead of a MsgPack diagnostic. The MsgPack019 doc states nesting types must be partial, but nothing enforces it. AC6 asks for a clear diagnostic and no broken code.
findings.scenario: `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] public partial class F<T> : IMessagePackFormatter<MyType> {}` produces no MsgPack diagnostic; the resolver emits `new global::F<T>()`, which does not compile. Likewise `class Outer { [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class F : IMessagePackFormatter<MyType> {} }` makes the generator emit `partial class Outer`, giving CS0260.

refs.quote: Any nesting types that contain the formatter must also be declared `partial`.

findings.suggestion: In Collect, reject formatters that are generic, abstract or static, lack an accessible parameterless constructor, are not accessible from the resolver, or have a non-partial containing type. Report MsgPack019 or a new diagnostic for each, and add tests.

findings.title: Explicit callback-receiver implementations are not detected, so the cast is never emitted
findings.body: `needsCast` looks for methods with explicit interface implementations whose Name equals "OnBeforeSerialize" or "OnAfterDeserialize". Roslyn names explicitly implemented methods with the interface qualifier (for example `MessagePack.IMessagePackSerializationCallbackReceiver.OnBeforeSerialize`), so the comparison never matches and needsCast is always false. The templates then emit `value.OnBeforeSerialize()`, which does not compile for an explicit implementation. The existing TypeCollector avoids this by casting whenever no member with the simple name exists. This also only inspects the type's own members, not base types.
findings.scenario: The formatted type is `class T : IMessagePackSerializationCallbackReceiver { void IMessagePackSerializationCallbackReceiver.OnBeforeSerialize() {} void IMessagePackSerializationCallbackReceiver.OnAfterDeserialize() {} public int X {get;set;} }`. The generated formatter contains `value.OnBeforeSerialize();` and fails with CS1061.
findings.suggestion: Mirror TypeCollector: `needsCastOnBefore = !type.GetMembers("OnBeforeSerialize").Any()` and the same for OnAfterDeserialize, or compare against `ExplicitInterfaceImplementations[i].Name`. Compute the two flags separately.

findings.title: A second formatter model for the same data type is silently dropped, leaving an empty partial class
findings.body: Generated-formatter models are added to the same ObjectInfos set as [MessagePackObject] models, and that set is keyed on DataType only. If the data type is also a [MessagePackObject] in the same compilation, or two [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] classes target the same T, the later model is discarded without a generator diagnostic. The discarded formatter's partial class gets no Serialize/Deserialize, so the build fails with CS0535 and no explanation. Because these formatters are excluded from KnownFormatters, the generator's own collision handling does not see them.
findings.scenario: `[MessagePackObject] class T { [Key(0)] public int X {get;set;} }` plus `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class TF : IMessagePackFormatter<T> {}` in the same project. The TypeCollector model is added first and wins; TF gets no body and fails with CS0535, and no MsgPack diagnostic names the conflict.

refs.quote: public int Compare(ResolverRegisterInfo x, ResolverRegisterInfo y) => x.DataType.CompareTo(y.DataType);

findings.suggestion: Detect duplicate data types among generated-formatter requests and against collected [MessagePackObject] types, and report a diagnostic. Decide explicitly which formatter wins.

findings.title: Tests miss AC2 body-less form, generated-output checks and several negative paths
findings.body: Every formatter in the tests is declared with `{ }`; the `partial class F : IMessagePackFormatter<T>;` form required by AC2 is never compiled, and the generator tests default to C# 7.3 where it is not legal. The six generator tests cover only rejection paths, so there is no positive generator test or snapshot of the emitted formatter and resolver. The NoDeserializingConstructor, MemberNeedsKey, KeysMustBeUnique, generic-data-type and inaccessible-type branches of the collector have no test. The surrogate execution test asserts only the array length (8) and a round trip through the same formatter, so it would still pass if Id and Name were written to the wrong slots symmetrically.
findings.scenario: Swap the int keys in CreateSurrogateMembers (e.g. always use members.Count as intKey while keeping MaxKey at 7): SurrogateControlsKeysAndMembership still passes because both directions agree. Break handling of the `;` body-less declaration: no test fails.
findings.suggestion: Add a body-less `;` declaration (generator test with LanguageVersion 12+ or in the execution project). Assert the exact bytes or slot positions for the surrogate case (nil at 0-2, Id at 3, Name at 7). Add a positive generator test with expected generated sources, and negative tests for the untested diagnostic branches.

refusals.question: Is a consumer-side surrogate type (plus a contractless default) an acceptable answer to the open question of how keys are annotated, given that the requirement listed DataMember, name-matched user-defined attributes, or generator-emitted attributes?
refusals.why: The requirement leaves the mechanism open and the PR picks a fourth option that was not listed. This is a product and API-shape decision that becomes public surface (`SurrogateType`) and is hard to change after release.

options.label: Accept surrogate-only
options.consequence: Project A stays untouched, but the wire contract lives in Project B and can drift from the type. Attributes on the type itself (including ignore markers) are disregarded, and AC4 is met only under a loose reading.

options.label: Require attributes on the type to be honoured as well
options.consequence: The collector must also read DataMember and/or name-matched Key/IgnoreMember on the formatted type. This is more work and needs precedence rules between type attributes and the surrogate.

options.label: Replace the surrogate with one of the listed mechanisms
options.consequence: The `SurrogateType` property and MsgPack022 are removed before they ship; this is a larger rework of the PR.

refusals.context: CreateContractlessMembers and CreateSurrogateMembers never call GetAttributes on members of the formatted type. The new public API is GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute.SurrogateType in MessagePack.Annotations.

refusals.question: Is it acceptable that the default (no surrogate) mode silently omits read-only members, private-setter members and constructor-only state, and reports no diagnostic for the dropped data?
refusals.why: Whether silent data loss on round-trip is tolerable, versus an error or warning per skipped member, is a risk-appetite and product decision. The requirement explicitly leaves the fallback behaviour for unannotated types open.

options.label: Keep silent skipping
options.consequence: Simple types work with zero configuration; immutable or record-style types round-trip with missing data and no build-time signal.

options.label: Warn or error on skipped public members
options.consequence: Users learn at build time what is not serialized; more diagnostics are needed plus a way to suppress them, for example through the surrogate.

options.label: Require a surrogate (no contractless default)
options.consequence: The wire contract is always explicit; the one-line usage in the requirement no longer works without extra code.

refusals.context: IsPublicReadWrite requires a public getter and a public setter (or a non-readonly public field). Constructor parameters are never matched (constructorParameters is always empty). The README lists this as a limitation; no diagnostic is emitted.

refusals.question: Is it acceptable that member types of the external type (enums, arrays, generic collections, other external types) get no generated formatters or resolver registrations, unlike members of [MessagePackObject] types?
refusals.why: This decides whether the feature is usable under AOT or without a dynamic resolver. It is a scope and support-matrix decision the requirement leaves open ("is a subset acceptable?").

options.label: Accept as a documented limitation
options.consequence: Works when StandardResolver or another dynamic resolver is in the chain; under AOT or Unity IL2CPP, such members fail at run time with a missing-formatter error.

options.label: Require member type collection
options.consequence: The collector must feed member types through TypeCollector.CollectCore so enum, array and generic formatters are generated and registered; larger change.

refusals.context: GeneratedFormatterCollector returns a model containing only the single ObjectSerializationInfo. The execution tests compose GeneratedMessagePackResolver with StandardResolver, so they do not exercise an AOT-only resolver chain.
